title: Getaways Guides: El Zonte
content_html:
Welcome to El Zonte, the vibrant beach town that seamlessly combines the relaxed atmosphere of coastal living with the innovative spirit of Bitcoin Beach. This small community is known for its friendly locals and year-round surfing opportunities. Spend enough time here, and you’ll soon be on a first-name basis with everyone—from the local fishermen to small business owners. Whether you’re visiting to surf, enjoy local cuisine, or explore the unique community, this guide will help you make the most of your stay.

Where to Stay

Zonset Surf Residences

If you’re looking for a comfortable and modern place to stay in El Zonte, our curated selection of condos at Zonset Surf Residences offers the perfect home base.

Developed by Bambu Development, Zonset Surf Residences is a brand-new project designed to meet the growing demand for modern coastal living in Surf City. Located on the second row from the beach, the development features three residential towers with select units offering ocean views. Residents and guests enjoy amenities such as a pool deck, gym, common lounge areas, surfboard storage, parking, 24/7 security, and easy beach access—creating a comfortable environment for both vacation stays and longer-term living.

Whether you’re visiting to surf, work remotely, or simply relax by the ocean, these listings provide a great way to experience El Zonte:

  • Zonte Surfside Getaway | 2B / 2BA Oceanview Condo in El Zonte
  • The Nomad Getaway | 1B / 1BA Surf Condo Perfect for Remote Work & Surf
  • Golden Hour Getaway | 2B / 2BA Oceanview Condo in El Zonte
  • The Zonte Sol Getaway | Cozy 1B / 1BA Surf Condo Steps Away from the Beach

Each unit offers a modern layout with thoughtful design, providing a relaxed and practical stay just steps from one of El Salvador’s most iconic surf breaks.

Morning Bliss: Sunrise, Surf, and Breakfast at Tecos

Begin your day early by witnessing a breathtaking sunrise over the ocean. After soaking in the view, grab your surfboard or rent one from local spots like Tres Hermanos, Esencia Nativa, or Puro Surf, which also offer lessons for beginners. Surf enthusiasts will find waves for every skill level—whether it’s the right-hand point break for advanced surfers or the left-hand beach break. Once you’ve worked up an appetite, head to Tecos, a local favorite in front of El Zonte’s iconic surf point. Enjoy a típico salvadoreño breakfast—a traditional Salvadoran meal that’s both delicious and satisfying—to fuel you for the adventures ahead.

Where to Eat & Drink

Lunch at Olas Permanentes

Savor the coastal flavors at Olas Permanentes, the perfect lunch spot for seafood lovers. Their ceviches are always a favorite, offering an authentic taste of the local cuisine. With the ocean right in front, it’s not just a place to eat—it’s a place to experience. Take a refreshing swim while you wait for your food and enjoy the unique charm of dining where Bitcoin is accepted.

Dinner at La Cajita Kitchen

For dinner, head to La Cajita Kitchen — a laid-back spot with beautiful views of the El Zonte river and the waves. Influenced by Chef Ricky of El Encanto and its French owners, the menu blends international flavors with local charm. Enjoy incredible crêpes, salmon pasta, and satisfying burgers, paired with refreshing drinks while watching the sunset. The restaurant also accepts Bitcoin, adding a modern touch to the experience.

Coffee with an ocean view

Looking for the perfect place to unwind with coffee? Visit Nan-tal, a cozy spot located inside Palo Verde Hotel, offering stunning ocean views. Relax to the sound of waves as you sip on your favorite brew. Don’t miss their special treat: artisanal plantain ice cream, a unique local delight that comes highly recommended! Nan-tal also serves delicious breakfast and dinner, making it a great place to enjoy a full day of relaxing and indulging.

Jeisi’s Pupuseria

Jeisi’s Pupuseria is renowned for serving some of the best pupusas in town. This family-owned eatery offers a wide variety of pupusas, including traditional corn and rice options, as well as unique vegan choices like garlic-flavored pupusas. Despite being busy, the friendly staff and delicious, affordable food make it worth the wait. Prices range from 75 cents to $1.50 per pupusa. Oh, and a quick heads-up: they take a well-deserved break on Wednesdays, so plan your pupusa cravings accordingly!

Attractions to Visit

Explore the El Zonte Caves

For adventure seekers, the El Zonte caves are a must-visit and truly a one-of-a-kind hidden gem. To find them, when you are facing the ocean, walk to your right along the beach, all the way to the end. You’ll cross a rock formation, and just beyond it, you’ll discover the caves. Be sure to plan your visit during low tide for safe exploration!

Skate Park

El Zonte Skate Bowl is the perfect place for the whole family. This vibrant skate park offers a dynamic space where kids, locals, and the skate community can gather, practice tricks, and enjoy the thrill of the sport. Beyond being a hub for skaters, the space also hosts events organized by the community and local brands, including memorable gatherings by Grlswirl. It’s an energetic hangout spot that brings fun and connection to the area, making it a must-visit for anyone in El Zonte. Plus, you’ll find the public beach entrance here.

Bitcoin-Friendly Local Shops

El Zonte is leading the way in Bitcoin adoption, as many local shops accept Bitcoin as a payment method. Whether you’re purchasing fresh vegetables, eggs, beer, water, or even a pair of shorts, it provides a seamless opportunity to witness the digital currency revolution in action.

Learn at the Bitcoin Beach Office

Discover how Bitcoin is empowering communities in El Salvador. Visit the Bitcoin Beach Office, where you can learn about inspiring local initiatives and the broader impact of Bitcoin in the area.

Visit the Bitcoin Hardware Store

The Bitcoin Hardware Store embodies El Zonte’s innovative spirit. This unique establishment offers a variety of products, including hardware wallets, seed metals, textbooks, business terminals, and fun merchandise. They also provide Bitcoin integration and recovery services, making it a valuable resource for newcomers and seasoned Bitcoin enthusiasts. The store also features a Bitcoin Lightning ATM, offering a convenient way to buy or interact with Bitcoin on-site.

Tips & Advice

  • Need to cross the river? The new bridge in El Zonte, located right on the street in front of El Vikingo restaurant, allows residents and visitors to cross the river with ease. It provides safe and convenient access between different parts of the community, making it easier to explore all that El Zonte has to offer.
  • ATM Location: For your banking needs, the only ATM in El Zonte is conveniently located right next to La Canasta Shop. This ensures locals and tourists can easily access cash without venturing far from the heart of town.
  • Local events and meetups: Look out for local events that might align with your stay. Every Friday night there is a Bitcoin dinner and the last Friday of every month a Bitcoin meetup at Palo Verde hotel. You will also find plenty of other activities and classes like yoga at sunset, salsa classes and more. Simply ask around town and you’re sure to figure out what’s happening.

Breathtaking Sunsets

End your day by witnessing one of El Zonte’s breathtaking sunsets—nature’s masterpiece that never fails to inspire awe. The best spots to soak in the magic are at the Bocana of the river or right in front of Olas Permanentes. From October to March, you can even catch the sun setting directly into the ocean, creating a truly unforgettable view. It’s moments like this that lead most visitors to ‘extend their stay’. Enjoy!

title: Solo Female Travel in El Salvador: Your Ultimate Guide
content_html:
El Salvador is one of Central America's best-kept secrets — and solo female travelers who make the trip keep saying the same thing: it completely exceeded their expectations.

Warm locals, world-class surf, volcanic landscapes, colonial towns, and sunsets over the Pacific. Here's everything you need to know to plan your trip.

Is It Safe?

Yes. In April 2025, the U.S. State Department upgraded El Salvador to a Level 1 travel advisory — the best possible rating, shared with France and Japan. The country has undergone one of the most remarkable safety transformations in the region, and women visiting today consistently report feeling comfortable and welcome.

Getting Here: Airport Transfer

The first thing to sort is your ride from the airport. Skip the stress of figuring it out on arrival — we offer private airport transfers straight to your accommodation in El Zonte or anywhere along the coast. It's the smoothest way to start your trip.

Book your transfer → getaways@goodlifeelsalvador.com

Where to Go

El Zonte

Your home base. A laid-back surf village with world-class waves, beachfront restaurants, and a welcoming mix of locals, expats, and international travelers. Safe, walkable, and genuinely beautiful.

El Tunco

10 minutes from El Zonte and a bit livelier. Great surf schools, beach bars, and easy to meet other travelers. Perfect for a day trip or a night out.

Suchitoto

A colonial gem about 90 minutes from San Salvador. Cobblestone streets, art galleries, and lake views. A completely different pace — do it as an overnight trip.

Ruta de las Flores

A scenic highland route connecting charming coffee towns, waterfalls, and local markets. The towns of Ataco and Apaneca are highlights. Best done over two days.

Santa Ana Volcano

The highest volcano in El Salvador with a stunning emerald crater lake at the top. Book a guided hike and go early — the views are worth every step.

Getting Around

  • Uber is available everywhere and costs $3–8 for most trips. Download it before you arrive.
  • Between towns, private shuttles and tour operators are your most comfortable option.
  • Along the coast, everything is within walking distance or a short ride away.
  • If you prefer to explore at your own pace, car and bike rentals are widely available. They typically start at around $25 per day, making it easy to visit different parts of the country.

Learn to Surf

Surf City 1 is one of the best places in the world to learn to surf. Beaches like El Zonte, El Sunzal, and San Blas offer consistent waves, warm water, and plenty of experienced local instructors. Solo women taking surf lessons is one of the biggest travel trends right now, and for good reason. It's a great way to meet people, build confidence in the water, and come home with a story worth telling.

Coffee Shops Are Your Best Friend

Solo travel and a good coffee shop go hand in hand — a safe, relaxed spot to work, journal, or just watch the world go by. El Salvador has some of the best coffee in the world, and the café scene reflects it.

  • In San Salvador: LUMA and Alquimia are two standout spots. At LUMA, don't miss their sourdough specialties, which have become a favorite among locals. Alquimia has earned international recognition for the quality of its coffee and its dedication to showcasing Salvadoran beans.
  • On the coast: Smaller cafés like Surf Café in El Tunco and Cocoa Café in El Zonte offer a cozy atmosphere, excellent coffee, and refreshing drinks. They're perfect places to settle in with your laptop, catch up on work, or enjoy a slow morning just steps from the beach.

Where to Stay

A self-contained apartment in El Zonte is the perfect solo base — your own space, your own kitchen, full freedom to come and go. At Getaways El Salvador, we have a curated selection of oceanfront and second-row condos, from cozy 1-bedroom to larger spaces for longer stays or remote work.

Browse our properties →

Quick Tips

  • Download WhatsApp — drivers, restaurants, everything runs on it here.
  • The dollar is the currency, and Bitcoin is a tender too, so if you're carrying BTC you can use it at plenty of spots in around the country.
  • Bring reef-safe sunscreen — the Pacific sun is intense, and the reefs will thank you.
  • Pack a light scarf — useful for visiting churches, cooler highland evenings, and long bus rides.
  • Learn a few words of Spanish — locals love the effort and it goes a long way.

title: Best Co-Working Spots and Cafés with WiFi in El Tunco
content_html:
El Tunco doesn't look like a remote work hub at first glance. But spend a few days on La Libertad coast and you'll figure out pretty quickly that it has some of the best spots to actually sit down, get online, and get things done.

Here's what we'd recommend.

Surf Cafe

The one most people find first, and for good reason. Surf Cafe has the right combination of reliable WiFi, good coffee, and a crowd that's used to people working — nobody's watching the clock or hovering around your table. The menu runs from breakfast through lunch, the atmosphere is easy, and it holds up for a full morning session without feeling like you need to justify being there. A solid default.

Nómada

The setup is clearly built with remote workers in mind — the layout works, the internet is strong, and the people there are generally doing the same thing you are. It has a bit more of a coworking feel than a café feel, which depending on what you need, is exactly the point. Good place to go when you have a deadline or just need a few uninterrupted hours.

Dale Dale Cafe

A different kind of stop. Dale Dale is less about the workspace setup and more about the coffee and the crowd — it draws a mix of locals and travelers, it moves at its own pace, and it's the kind of place you tend to stay longer than planned. WiFi works fine. It's better suited to a slower afternoon than a back-to-back meeting day, but as a place to decompress mid-week or get some writing done, it earns its spot on the list.

Tusell Tostadores

For anyone who takes coffee seriously, this one stands out. Tusell is a specialty roaster — single origins, proper brewing, the kind of place where the product actually reflects what's on the menu. The space is comfortable, it's a bit quieter and fresher with the AC, than the other beachfront options; also, the WiFi holds up. If you're going to be staring at a screen for four hours, you might as well have a genuinely good cup in front of you.

A Few Things Worth Knowing

Mornings are consistently the best time to go — quieter, cooler, and you'll have your pick of seats. By early afternoon on weekends things fill up, so plan accordingly.

From El Zonte side of the coast, an Uber gets you there for $3–5. Most drivers know these spots by name, but they can't take you to the coffee shop directly since you are only able to get there on foot. There's a pick up spot where you can take the uber in El Zonte and there's another spot in El Tunco where you will be dropped off, then you will have to walk to your destination coffee shop. Fortunately, none of them are far from each other!

However, is worth checking their available hours on Instagram before you go; sometimes, schedules on the coast don't always follow what's listed online.

The practical case for working remotely from El Salvador is straightforward — solid internet along the coast, good weather year-round, and the ocean close enough that a surf session between calls is a realistic option.

title: Canegue Cafe: The Best Spot for Brunch in El Zonte
content_html:
El Zonte doesn't have a long list of brunch spots. It doesn't need one. What it has is Canegue Cafe — and once you've been, it's pretty much the only answer to the question of where to go on a slow morning.

It's the kind of place that earns its reputation quietly. No gimmicks, no oversized menus trying to be everything. Just good food, good coffee, and a setting that makes it easy to stay longer than you planned.

The Food

Brunch in a surf town can go one of two ways — either it's an afterthought, or someone actually cared about putting it together. Canegue is the second kind. The menu is focused, which is usually a good sign. What's on it is done well, and the portions make sense for people who have either just come out of the water or are about to go in.

The coffee is worth ordering twice. El Salvador produces some of the best beans in the region, and Canegue treats that seriously. Whether you're starting with an Americano before the rest of the table arrives or working through a slow pour-over while you watch the street wake up, it holds up.

The Setting

El Zonte has a particular energy in the morning: unhurried, a little golden, the kind of pace that makes you want to put your phone down. Canegue fits that perfectly. The space feels thought through without feeling designed. It's comfortable in the way that places get comfortable when the people running them actually use them.

It draws a mix of people — locals, long-term residents, travelers passing through, remote workers getting a head start on the day. The crowd tends to be relaxed, and the vibe follows. You're not going to feel rushed or out of place whether you're there for forty minutes or two hours.

When to Go

Mornings are the move. Get there early enough and you'll have your pick of spots. By mid-morning on weekends it fills up, and for good reason. If you're staying nearby, it's an easy walk — the kind of morning routine that makes you understand why people end up staying in El Zonte longer than they originally planned.

The Honest Take

There are places that are good and places that become part of your routine. Canegue is the second kind. If you're spending any time on the La Libertad coast, it's worth building a morning around.

If you're thinking about a longer stay in El Zonte — a week, a month, or something more open-ended — our apartments are close enough to make this your regular spot.

title: Best Surf Schools in Surf City, El Salvador
content_html:
"Surf City" is the stretch of La Libertad coastline that runs from Punta Roca to Mizata — a string of black-sand beaches with a break for almost every level, minutes apart from each other by bus or car. El Tunco has the rockier, more advanced breaks and the busiest nightlife; El Zonte is quieter, with a friendlier point break and most of its life centered on one main street; San Blas is smaller still, a beach break most people only reach on a day trip from one of the other two.

That geography matters more than any single school's reputation. Which one makes sense for you depends less on which name you've heard and more on where you're staying, how many days you have, whether you've surfed before, and whether you want one lesson or a full week of coaching. Here's what each of these five actually looks like on the ground.

Puro Surf — El Zonte

Puro Surf sits right on El Zonte point, and it's built around structure: ISA-certified coaches, daily check-ins before paddling out, and video review after each session so you can see what your coach is talking about.

The weekly surf camp format includes coaching, board selection with your coach, and afternoon add-ons like yoga, mobility work, or an ice bath. Coaches assign you a board for the week, and you're free to take it out for extra solo sessions between lessons if the swell is working. It's set up for people who want to actually change their surfing over several days, not just stand up once and call it a win.

Good for: intermediate surfers or committed beginners who want a full week of coaching.

Los 3 Hermanos Surf — El Zonte

A local, family-run school on El Zonte beach — the name refers to the three brothers who run it. Lessons are taught in Spanish, English, and French.

What comes up most in feedback is that instructors stay close in the water instead of drifting off to catch their own waves — which matters more than it sounds like when you're a beginner trying to time a wave and could use someone right next to you calling it. Lessons here tend to run at El Zonte's main point break, though for beginners they'll sometimes drive you over to Palmarcito or La Paz , a gentler, more forgiving wave a short trip down the coast.

Board, bodyboard, and skateboard rentals run alongside the lessons, and they'll also set up kayak or stand-up paddle trips if you want a day off from surfing without leaving the water.

Good for: a single lesson or a couple of sessions, especially if you want an instructor who stays close and won't leave you to figure out timing on your own.

Surfing Your Fears — El Zonte

This one is coaching for people who already know how to surf but feel stuck. The approach treats a stalled plateau as partly technical and partly mental, and lessons work through both: reading your specific fear or hesitation alongside the actual mechanics of your pop-up or bottom turn.

From April to October, when south swells start lighting up the east side of the country, they'll also run custom trips out to Las Flores and Punta Mango, about 3.5 hours from El Zonte, chasing right-hand point breaks that don't show up on the standard El Zonte-El Tunco lesson circuit. That's a different kind of session than a first-timer lesson — it assumes you're already comfortable in the water and want to push past a specific block, whether that's committing to a bigger wave, cleaning up a bottom turn, or just getting past the hesitation that keeps you stuck at the same level.

Sessions are built around conversation as much as water time — understanding what's actually holding you back before adjusting the technical side. If you've had multiple lessons elsewhere and feel like you've hit a wall, this is coaching aimed specifically at that wall rather than another round of the basics.

Good for: surfers who've plateaued and want coaching aimed at a specific mental or technical sticking point.

Wayo Surf School — El Tunco

Wayo is based in the center of El Tunco. It covers more ground than most: surf lessons, board and wetsuit rental, a surf shop, scooter and motorcycle rental, lofts to stay in, and day trips to Tamanique waterfalls, Santa Ana volcano, and the Ruta de las Flores.

Private lessons run higher than the average one-hour session elsewhere on this stretch — but they come with instructors who surf at a competitive level, and a private session is the format most people book rather than a group class.

Wayo works more like a one-stop shop for people staying independently in El Tunco: rent a scooter to get around, rent a board for the days you don't want a lesson, and book the transfer to and from the airport through the same place.

Good for: anyone based in El Tunco who wants surfing, board rentals, transfers, and day trips in one place.

Surf Strong — Playa San Blas

Located in Playa San Blas, about 7 minutes from El Tunco. San Blas has a sandy bottom and a beach break that's genuinely easier on beginners than the rockier breaks in El Tunco itself — a lot of whitewater to practice in before you're dealing with a real takeoff.

It's a straightforward setup: board rentals and lessons, run by a local surfer, no bundled packages, no add-on services, no hotel attached. Rentals run around $10 for a full day if you'd rather practice on your own than take a formal lesson.

Good for: a first surf lesson ever, or a low-key rental day.

Good to know

  • Pricing runs a wide range. A single group lesson typically falls between $25 and $45, private lessons at the higher end can run $60 or more, and board rentals alone are usually $10-15 a day. Multi-day academy packages like Puro Surf's are priced separately and include lodging.
  • Cash and card both work, but small operators lean cash. El Zonte was one of the first places in the country to accept bitcoin, so some smaller shops and schools can take it — worth asking directly rather than assuming.
  • Distances are short but not walkable in the heat. El Tunco, El Zonte, and San Blas are all within about 15-20 minutes of each other by local bus or tuk-tuk — useful if the school you want is based in a different town than where you're staying.
  • Bring reef-safe sunscreen and a rash guard. Sessions often run 60-90 minutes in direct sun, and boards and wetsuits are provided by every school on this list, so there's no need to bring your own gear unless you already have a board you're attached to.
  • Ask about instructor-to-student ratio before booking a group lesson. It varies a lot between schools, and it's the single biggest factor in how much individual attention you'll actually get in the water.

Whichever school you end up with, staying close to the break makes the actual difference — a two-minute walk to the water in the morning beats a bus ride, every time. Take a look at Getaways rentals along the coast before you book anything else.

title: El Salvador: Everything You Need to Know Before Visiting
content_html:
We get some version of the same message every week: "We're thinking about El Salvador. What do we actually need to know?" So here it is, all in one place, from someone who actually lives here.

Before You Fly

Most visitors (US, Canada, UK, EU, and plenty of others) don't need a visa for stays under 90 days, just a passport stamp at the airport. Make sure your passport has at least six months of validity left. San Salvador's international airport (SAL) is the main entry point, about 45 minutes to an hour from the La Libertad coast, and the newer Pacific terminal has made things noticeably smoother for beach-focused arrivals. Direct flights run from several US hubs: Houston, Miami, Los Angeles, Dallas, Atlanta; so depending on where you're starting, you might not need a connection at all.

Once you're here, the US dollar is the official currency, so there's no exchanging money or doing conversion math. Cards are widely accepted in restaurants and hotels, but keep some cash on hand for tuk-tuks and local markets, and Spanish is the official language, though English is common in tourist areas along the coast. A little Spanish still goes a long way with locals.

Is It Safe? When Should You Go?

This is what everyone actually wants to know, so plainly: El Salvador's security situation has changed dramatically over the past few years, and that shift is well documented — it's a big part of why so many more travelers are showing up now. Still, use the same common sense you'd use anywhere: mind your surroundings at night, stick to well-traveled areas. The coast has a relaxed, welcoming feel, full of cafés, coworkers, and other travelers.

As for timing, there are two seasons here, not four: dry season (roughly November through April) brings consistent sun and busier crowds, while rainy season (May through October) usually means sunny mornings with afternoon showers, a greener landscape, and better surf swells for some. Temperatures stay warm year-round, typically in the 80s°F, so pack light regardless of when you come.

Getting Around and Where to Stay

A rental car gives you the most freedom if you're planning to explore beyond one town, though if you're basing yourself in one spot on the coast (which I'd recommend for a first trip) tuk-tuks and short shuttle rides will cover most of what you need. For beach life and a slower pace, the La Libertad coast is the move: El Tunco has more energy and nightlife, El Zonte is quieter with a wellness and remote-work scene. San Salvador is worth a day trip for museums or city history, but most visitors treat it as a transit point rather than a base.

If you'd rather skip the guesswork on where to stay, we have units scattered along this stretch of coast: walking distance to the breaks, cafés, and coworking spots mentioned above. Each one's set up with fast wifi, a kitchen if you'd rather not eat out every meal, and someone local to point you toward whatever you're looking for, whether that's a quiet beach or a good ceviche spot.

Practical Extras

Wifi is reliable in hotels, cafés, and the growing number of coworking spaces along the country, and local SIM cards are cheap and easy to grab at the airport. Tipping is 10% at sit-down restaurants — check the bill first, since it's sometimes already included.

For packing: reef-safe sunscreen, a light rain jacket if you're visiting in rainy season, sandals plus one sturdy pair of shoes for hikes or volcanoes, small bills for tuk-tuks and markets, and a reusable water bottle.

Day Trips and Tours

Getting out for the day is easy too — the volcanoes inland, like Santa Ana or Izalco, make for a solid change of scenery from the coast, and tours can usually be arranged with a local guide rather than booked cold online. We offer concierge services for guests who'd rather not sort out logistics themselves, just let us know what you're interested in and we'll help arrange the guide, transport, or timing.

Surf Year-Round

If surfing's part of the draw, there's no real off-season here — swells run year-round, they just shift in character with the seasons. El Tunco and El Zonte both have their own personality as breaks, and there are a handful of quieter spots further down the coast worth exploring if you're past beginner and want less of a crowd.

One Last Thing

The best trips here aren't the rushed ones. Give yourself time to sit at a café, watch a sunset from the same spot twice, and let a town grow on you before moving to the next one.

title: 7 Mistakes to Avoid When Booking a Vacation Rental
content_html:
Most of what goes wrong on a trip traces back to a booking decision made weeks earlier, usually in a hurry. Here's what we see most often, and how to skip it.

1. Booking based on photos alone

A wide-angle lens makes a small room look like a suite. Before you commit, don't just count the rooms—check the square footage. If a listing only shows sunset shots and no interior angles of the bathroom or kitchen, ask for them. Hosts who have nothing to hide will send them without hesitation.

2. Ignoring the actual distance to the beach

"Steps from the beach" gets used loosely. Some properties are a two-minute walk down a sand path. Others are a fifteen-minute walk down a hill you'll have to climb back up in the heat, with your board under one arm. Ask for the exact walking time, not the listing's version of it, and factor in whether that walk is flat, stepped, or unpaved.

3. Not asking about road access

La Libertad's coastal road is beautiful and, in places, rough. Some rentals sit down dirt tracks that a regular sedan won't love after rain. If you're renting a car, ask directly whether the access road is paved and whether 4x4 is recommended. This one detail changes what car you book.

4. Overlooking who else is on the property

A lot of coastal rentals share land with other units, a restaurant, or a pool used by day guests. If quiet matters to you, ask what else operates on the same property and at what hours. If a lively shared space is what you want, ask that too. Neither is wrong, but you want to know which one you're getting.

5. Skipping the WiFi and power question

Power along the coast is generally reliable, but not universal, and WiFi speed varies a lot property to property. If you need to work during your trip, ask for the actual megabit speed, not just "yes, we have WiFi." A rental with strong signal and stable power is a different trip than one without.

6. Booking without checking cancellation terms

Weather on this coast can shift plans, and so can flights. Read the cancellation policy before you book, not after something changes. Some hosts are flexible with advance notice; others hold firm. Knowing which one you're dealing with removes a stress you don't need on vacation.

7. Not confirming what's actually included

Towels, drinking water, coffee, a working blender for the mornings you'll want a smoothie after a surf session — these details aren't always listed. A quick message before booking, asking what's stocked and what you should bring, saves a supply run on day one.

None of these mistakes are dramatic. They're just the small gaps between what a listing implies and what a property actually offers. A few direct questions before you book close that gap completely, and set up the rest of the trip to feel exactly like the version you pictured.

title: Why El Salvador Should Be Your Next Beach Destination
content_html:
El Salvador's coastline runs about 320 kilometers along the Pacific, and for a long time, most travelers passed over it. That's starting to change, and not because of a marketing push — it's the surf, the waves, and a stretch of coast that hasn't been packaged into resort towns yet.

The waves are the draw

El Zonte, Sunzal, and El Tunco are all within a short drive of each other, and each has a different personality. El Zonte is quieter, known for its point break and black volcanic sand — a wave that holds its shape even when other spots get blown out. Sunzal is longer and more forgiving, good for people still finding their footing. El Tunco is livelier, with a heavier break near the rocks that draws locals and visiting surfers looking to test themselves.

La Libertad, the port town just past El Tunco, has its own point breaks — Punta Roca among them, a fast right-hander considered one of the best in the country and a regular stop on the competitive circuit. It's not a beginner wave, but it's part of why this stretch of coast has a real surf pedigree, not just a casual one.

Further east, Costa del Sol is known mostly for its calm, wide beaches — but tucked along that same coast is a wave that barely gets talked about outside of local surf circles, one that only shows up under the right swell and is generally left to the handful of pro-level surfers who know when to be there.

Past that, near La Unión, spots like Las Flores, El Cuco, and Punta Mango make up the east coast's surf stretch — long point breaks, fewer people, and a three-to-four-hour drive from San Salvador that keeps the crowds thin.

The coast is growing on its own terms

Compared to other Central American coastlines that went through fast, resort-driven development, El Salvador's beach towns are growing at a different pace — one shaped by the people who already live there. Streets are narrow, buildings are low, and a lot of what you'll eat comes from someone's family kitchen rather than a hotel restaurant. New rental homes and cafés are showing up, but they're going in next to existing family properties, not replacing them, and the sand stays public with no gated compounds cutting off beach access.

That's part of the appeal for travelers who've already done the more polished version of a beach vacation elsewhere and are looking for a place that's still shaping its own identity instead of one built to a template.

Getting there is easier than people assume

San Salvador's international airport is about an hour and a half from the coast by car. There's no multi-leg journey required — you land, and you're at the beach before dinner. Direct flights connect San Salvador to several major U.S. cities, including Miami, Houston, Los Angeles, and Dallas, so for a lot of travelers this isn't even a long-haul trip. Once you land, getting to the coast is straightforward: private shuttles and rental cars both make the drive easily, and the road from the airport runs close enough to the coastline that the ocean is visible well before you reach your destination. For a country that isn't yet on most people's shortlist, the logistics are surprisingly simple.

The food reflects the coast, not a tourist menu

Beachside food here tends to be small operations: a woman grilling fish a few steps from the sand, a pupusería that's been in the same spot for years, fresh coconut sold out of a cooler. Pupusas — thick corn tortillas filled with cheese, beans, or pork, cooked on a flat griddle — are the everyday staple, sold everywhere from roadside stands to sit-down comedores, usually for less than a dollar each.

Seafood follows the same pattern: whatever came in on the boats that morning is what's on the menu that day, often grilled whole with lime and a side of rice. It's not curated for visitors — it's what's already there, which is part of what makes it worth trying.

Practical things to know before you go

  • Dry season (November–April) brings the most consistent surf conditions and the least rain, the perfect time for you to learn to surf— this is also the busiest stretch, so rentals and popular spots book up further in advance.
  • Rainy season (May–October) still has plenty of sunny mornings — rain tends to arrive in the afternoon, often as a short, heavy downpour rather than an all-day event, and the coast is noticeably quieter and greener during these months. This is the best time for professional surfers since we have big waves to go in.
  • Rental cars and private shuttles are both common ways to get from the airport to the coast; public transport exists but takes longer and involves more transfers.
  • Cash and card are both widely accepted in the beach towns, along with Bitcoin in and around El Zonte. U.S. dollars are the official currency, which simplifies things for a lot of visitors and means no currency exchange is needed before the trip.

Right now, you can still show up at any beach, drop your bag, and be in the water within the hour: no line, no wristband, no one telling you where to stand. That's not going to be true forever.

If you're ready to see it for yourself, browse our rentals and find a place a few steps from the sand.

title: Covana Kitchen: Where to Eat in El Zonte, El Salvador
content_html:
Located inside Puro Surf Hotel, Covana Kitchen is open to both hotel guests and visitors. It's a popular breakfast and coffee spot in El Zonte, with a relaxed open-air setting just steps from the beach.

The Setting

Covana Kitchen features an open-air dining area with a large palm-thatched roof and views toward the Pacific. Just steps from the beach, it's designed to make the most of the ocean breeze and natural surroundings. Mornings tend to be the busiest, while afternoons are generally quieter and more relaxed.

The design leans into that natural setting rather than fighting it. Wood, thatch, open sightlines to the beach — nothing about the space feels imported or staged.

Breakfast

Breakfast here tends to run long. Carrot pancakes come up often as a favorite among regulars, alongside the usual eggs-and-fruit plates built for people about to go surf or just coming back from it. It's a solid coffee stop too, one of the better ones in town if you're working remotely for the morning and want something more substantial than a café pastry.

Lunch and Dinner

The lunch and dinner menu combines Salvadoran ingredients with a variety of international dishes. Options include tuna poke bowls, seafood pasta, fish tacos, coconut seafood soup, and ceviche, along with other fresh seafood and seasonal specials. Whether you're stopping by after the beach or meeting friends for dinner, the menu offers a range of choices for different tastes.

The kitchen doesn't seem interested in choosing a single lane — global techniques and local ingredients.

Service and Atmosphere

Service is friendly and attentive, and the atmosphere varies throughout the day. Mornings are typically quieter, while lunch and dinner attract a larger crowd of locals and visitors. Weekends are often the busiest, particularly during peak meal times.

Good for Families and Remote Workers

Covana ends up working for two very different kinds of visitors, often at the same time. Families find it easy, the open layout gives kids room to move, and the menu has enough range that picky and adventurous eaters both find something. For remote workers, the ocean view, decent coffee, and open-air setting make it an easy spot to post up with a laptop for a few hours instead of working from a rental with limited outdoor space.

Getting There

Covana Kitchen sits inside Puro Surf Hotel at Km 52 on the Carretera del Litoral, right on Playa El Zonte. If you're staying anywhere along the El Zonte stretch, it's an easy walk for most rentals in the area — no car needed, and it's one of the few spots in town where you can eat well without leaving the sound of the waves. For visitors coming from elsewhere along the coast or from San Salvador, it's a straightforward stop along the Litoral highway, easy to find and well known enough locally that directions are rarely necessary once you're in town.

Good to Know

Open daily, roughly 7:30 AM–9:00 PM Sunday through Thursday, and 7:30 AM–10:00 PM Friday and Saturday. Open to the public, not just hotel guests. Reservations aren't strictly necessary for most meals, but worth considering for dinner on weekends when the crowd picks up. If you're new to El Zonte, it's a solid first stop for orienting yourself — a good meal, a view of the water, and a sense of the town's pace before you head out to explore the rest of the beach.

If you're planning a longer stay nearby, browsing our rentals within walking distance of Covana Kitchen and the rest of El Zonte's beach front is worth doing before you book — it makes mornings like this one part of the routine instead of a special trip.
